# 2026 Federal Tax Brackets Explained

Many workers worry that getting a raise will push them into a higher tax bracket and reduce their take-home pay. That is one of the most common myths about U.S. income taxes — crossing into a higher [tax bracket](/federal-tax-brackets) never lowers your net income.

## How Tax Brackets Actually Work

The United States uses a **progressive** income tax system, meaning your **taxable income** (gross income minus deductions) is taxed in layers rather than all at one flat rate.

For example, suppose you are a single filer with $60,000 of **taxable income** in 2026 (roughly $76,100 gross after the $16,100 standard deduction):

- Your first $12,400 is taxed at **10%** ($1,240).
- Income from $12,401 to $50,400 is taxed at **12%** ($4,560).
- Only the remaining $9,600 (from $50,401 to $60,000) is taxed at **22%** ($2,112).

Only the dollars *above* each threshold get the higher rate. Your **marginal tax rate** — the rate on your last dollar of taxable income — is 22%, while your **effective federal tax rate** (total federal tax ÷ gross income) is much lower (around 10.4% on $76,100 gross).

## Official 2026 Brackets for Single Filers (IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-32)

Here are the official 2026 federal income tax brackets for single filers:

- **10%** on taxable income up to $12,400
- **12%** from $12,401 to $50,400
- **22%** from $50,401 to $105,700
- **24%** from $105,701 to $201,775
- **32%** from $201,776 to $256,225
- **35%** from $256,226 to $640,600
- **37%** on taxable income over $640,600

## Official 2026 Brackets for Married Filing Jointly

For married couples filing jointly in 2026, most brackets are double the single thresholds (up through 32%):

- **10%** on taxable income up to $24,800
- **12%** from $24,801 to $100,800
- **22%** from $100,801 to $211,400
- **24%** from $211,401 to $403,550
- **32%** from $403,551 to $512,450
- **35%** from $512,451 to $768,700
- **37%** on taxable income over $768,700

Note that the 35% and 37% joint thresholds are less than double the single thresholds, which can create a marriage penalty for high-earning dual-income couples.

## Official 2026 Standard Deductions

Before any brackets apply, the standard deduction reduces your gross income:

- **Single / Married Filing Separately**: $16,100
- **Married Filing Jointly**: $32,200
- **Head of Household**: $24,150

Most taxpayers claim the standard deduction rather than itemizing. If your mortgage interest, charitable donations, and deductible state/local taxes exceed the standard deduction, itemizing can lower your tax bill further. Use our [paycheck calculator](/paycheck-calculator) to see your exact 2026 take-home pay after federal, FICA, and state taxes.

## Key Takeaways

- **Marginal rate vs. effective rate**: Your marginal rate applies only to your top slice of taxable income. Your effective rate is always lower.
- **Standard deduction shield**: The $16,100 single ($32,200 joint) standard deduction means your first dollars of earned income owe $0 in federal income tax.
- **Pre-tax contributions reduce your top bracket**: Traditional [401(k) contributions](/401k-retirement-calculator) (up to $24,500 in 2026) and HSA deposits cut taxable income from your highest marginal bracket first.
- **Planning for next year**: See the official [2027 federal tax brackets](/tax-brackets-2027) (IRS Rev. Proc. 2026-35) to plan year-end income and deductions.
